A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Modal Aphasia study. The main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across additions, relocation, and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original movie-poster evaluations, controlled Janus-Pro/Harmon experiments, and a safety case study in Sections 3–5 and Appendices A–C.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds a visualization-prompt experiment in Appendix A.3 and base-model benchmark measurements in Table 5.

M1.justification: The model architectures, backbone-only fine-tuning, and two-stage safety-training procedure are unchanged. Appendix A.3 tests a visualization instruction as an experimental intervention; it does not introduce an adopted model component or revise the original training method.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same nine movie posters, 600 synthetic portraits, 840 abstract-concept images, safety dataset, auxiliary datasets, tinyMMLU, and GenEval. The additional prompting experiment retains the existing poster-description task and data.

E2.justification: Table 5 adds unfine-tuned Harmon and Janus-Pro as comparators on tinyMMLU and GenEval; v1 reports only fine-tuned variants there. The original model comparisons and Harmon control-task comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Appendix A.3 adds a visualization-first prompting protocol using the September 21 ChatGPT interface and GPT-5 Instant, while retaining the original August 22 auto-thinking experiment. It explicitly prohibits web search and regenerates the joint grading rubric to regrade reused images. These are additional experimental conditions, not replacements for the original settings.

E4.justification: New Appendix A.3 and Figure 8 test whether asking the model to visualize before describing avoids modal aphasia. Added base-model scores also strengthen the capability-preservation analysis in Appendix B.3. The existing concept analyses, Harmon ablations, and safety case study are retained.

E5.justification: The existing reporting of means and standard errors across three evaluation runs or training seeds is retained. New Figure 8 follows the same three-evaluation-run practice, and Table 5 extends the existing uncertainty format. No changed repetition counts or new statistical procedures are reported.

E6.justification: New Figure 8 reports approximately 35% text error versus 2% image error under the added prompting and grading conditions. Table 5 adds base-model tinyMMLU/GenEval scores of 0.430265/0.645570 for Harmon and 0.449397/0.737794 for Janus-Pro. Appendix A.1 also newly reports their failure to reproduce posters accurately. Existing plotted results and fine-tuned benchmark scores are unchanged; the new error rates do not establish a same-setting improvement over the original 45%/6%.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs. Existing mathematical specifications are unchanged, and the new architectural and mechanism discussion remains conceptual.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same central claims: visual knowledge can remain inaccessible through text, the phenomenon occurs in controlled multimodal experiments, and it can undermine unimodal safeguards. The added experiment supports the existing visualization-reasoning conjecture without redefining the principal contributions.

C2.justification: v2 removes 'from scratch' from the joint-training description and adds an explicit acknowledgment that GPT-5's architecture is unknown, followed by a speculative shared-representation argument in Appendix A.1. Appendix A.3 interprets failed visualization prompting as suggesting that deeper changes are needed. Appendix D adds distinctions from modality-convergence and in-context imbalance explanations.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 supplies the full additional prompt, interface date and mode, search restriction, and image-reuse/regrading procedure. Appendix B.3 specifies that base-model benchmarks use the fine-tuned models' inference setup. Existing training hyperparameters, dataset construction details, and code/data access statements remain unchanged.

R1.justification: New Appendix D substantially expands positioning against modality imbalance and visual/spatial commonsense research, supported by eight additional cited works. It explicitly distinguishes training-time access to memorized visual concepts from in-context modality dominance, differing convergence behavior, and broader commonsense generalization.

P1.justification: The main narrative is largely retained, with localized wording and caption refinements, corrected chance-level phrasing, and updated publication and acknowledgment text. Appendix A.3 and the related-work Appendix D are added; the unchanged LLM-use disclosure moves from D to E.

P2.justification: v2 adds the three-panel Figure 8, inserts dashed chance-level references into existing accuracy plots, and expands Table 5 with a base-model group. Subsequent figures are renumbered and appendix displays reflow. Existing plotted data and illustrative images are retained.

improvement.justification: The added base-model controls make fine-tuning effects easier to assess, the visualization-prompt experiment tests a previously untested suggestion, and Appendix D clarifies the relationship to closely related research. The gains are limited: the central evidence is unchanged, and the additional experiment's changed ChatGPT mode/date and regenerated rubric prevent isolating a causal prompting benefit.
